title: Variables, types and initialisation
goal: Set initial values, trace one update and explain why the other variables keep their values.

prerequisites.text: You can match %d, %c and the floating-point format to their arguments.

terms.title: Variable
terms.definition: A named object with a type and a value.

terms.title: Initialisation
terms.definition: Giving a variable its first value when it is created.

terms.title: Assignment
terms.definition: Storing a new value in an existing object. The expression is on the right and the destination is on the left.

sections.title: Data live separately from the format
paragraphs: A seat count is an integer, time has a fractional part, and a zone is a character. Use int seats, double time and char zone. Names distinguish their purpose and types determine operations and representation.
int seats = 6 defines a variable and supplies its first value. In seats = seats + 2, the right side reads the old 6 and computes 8. Then 8 is stored in the same variable.

C guarantees minimum type ranges, not one int size for every environment. The small values in these examples fit the minimum guaranteed range. double is useful for time measurements, but it cannot represent every decimal fraction exactly.

sections.title: Before and after a change
paragraphs: Trace the three values before the first print. After the assignment, identify which name and value pair changed.
steps: The declarations create and initialise values 6, A and 1.5.
The first printf prints the zone, the number of seats and time. Argument order follows the format.
seats = seats + 2 changes only seats. The second printf receives 8 and the unchanged values of the other variables.
trace: Read the old value and store the new one
These objects were not assigned to

sections.title: Obtain a value before reading it
paragraphs: A local int seats; with no value cannot yet be passed safely to printf. A local object is not automatically set to zero here. Initialise it or assign it a value before its first read.
Do not confuse assignment with a mathematical equality. seats = seats + 2 means update the object. It does not claim that the old and new values are equal.

sections.title: Trace the inventory
paragraphs: A loading line starts with a known number of boxes. Three are shipped, while the period and the line label stay the same. Use one output format and update the variable rather than typing a fixed second result.
Draw a small before-and-after table. It shows what stays constant even if you accidentally swap two printf arguments.

selfcheck.prompt: What changes in the second line of the example?
options: Seats become 8 with the same zone and time
feedback: Correct. The assignment changes only seats.

selfcheck.prompt: What fixes reading int seats; before it has a value?
options: Give seats a value before its first use
feedback: Correct. Define the value before reading it.
Changing another variable does not set seats.
A format does not initialise arguments.

selfcheck.prompt: Why do the two uses of seats in seats = seats + 2 refer to one variable?
selfcheck.feedback: The right side reads the previous value of the same object. The left side names where to store the result after evaluating the right side.

practice.title: Track boxes on a loading line
practice.task: Line B starts with 12 boxes and a period of 0.5 hours. Print B: 12 / 0.5 h. Reduce the count by three and print the second line using the same format.
criteria: The new count is 9 and is computed from the previous count.
The line and period stay unchanged.
All objects receive values before they are read.
practice.hint: Use the seats update as a guide. Here you subtract from boxes instead of adding.

steps.action: Record the before and after values.
steps.expected: B and 0.5 appear twice, while 12 changes to 9.

steps.action: Add both prints with the update between them.
steps.why: Execution goes from top to bottom.

steps.expected: After shipping, 12 remain and the line and period are unchanged.

exercises.title: Transfer the idea
exercises.task: Change only the period to 1.0, then change the line separately. Predict which parts of both lines change in each test.
criteria: Changing one initial value affects its own field in both prints.
